title: SSRF, Path Traversal & Deserialization
objectives: Restrict server-side URL fetching with scheme and host allowlists
Canonicalize and prefix-check file paths so traversal cannot escape the base directory
Explain why deserializing untrusted data can execute code, not just create objects
Prefer plain data formats with schema validation for anything crossing a trust boundary
body:
Three bugs where your server does exactly what it was asked — fetch a URL, read a file, rebuild an object — become attacks because the *requester* chose the input. The shared defense philosophy: the server decides the safe universe (allowed hosts, allowed directory, allowed types) and verifies the request fits inside it after canonicalization, not before.

## The problem
Your app fetches an image URL the user pastes, serves files from an uploads directory by name, and restores a saved session from a serialized blob. Each feature works; each also lets a crafted input aim the server somewhere you never intended — an internal metadata service, a file outside the uploads folder, or a payload that instantiates dangerous classes on load.

## Constraints
- The server can reach internal networks the user cannot — SSRF turns the server into a proxy for the attacker.
- Encoded and dotted path segments (`..`, `%2e%2e`) are aliases for the same escape; checking raw strings misses them.
- Canonicalization must happen *before* the prefix check: resolve to the absolute real path, then verify it sits inside the base.
- Data-format deserialization (`JSON.parse`) produces values; type-reconstructing serializers (language-native object graphs) can run code during load — the danger is reconstruction, not parsing.

## Options
```js
// SSRF: allowlist scheme + host, resolve and block private ranges
function urlAllowed(u) {
  const url = new URL(u)
  const ok =
    url.protocol === "https:" &&
    ["images.example.com", "cdn.example.com"].includes(url.hostname)
  return ok
}

// Path traversal: decode -> normalize -> prefix-check inside the base
function safeJoin(base, requested) {
  const segs = decodeURIComponent(requested).split("/")
    .filter((s) => s && s !== "." && s !== "..")   // no escape segments survive
  return base + "/" + segs.join("/")
}

// Deserialization: JSON + schema, never a type-reconstructing loader
const data = JSON.parse(raw)              // values only
require("zod").parse(schema, data)        // structure verified at the boundary
```
The traversal helper mirrors this very app's own content validator: decode percent-escapes, drop `.` and `..` segments, and never let the result leave the configured base directory.

## Tradeoffs
URL allowlists break whenever a partner domain changes and need a config process — the honest cost of not being an open proxy. Strict path canonicalization rejects symlink tricks and unusual encodings, occasionally refusing a legitimate odd filename. Schema validation adds a dependency and per-field effort, and buys the ability to reject malformed data with clear errors instead of undefined behavior.

## Decision
For outbound fetches: https-only, explicit host allowlist, and block responses that redirect into private ranges. For file access: canonicalize then prefix-check, and generate server-side filenames where possible so user input never becomes a path segment. For persisted structures: JSON plus schema validation; reserve native deserialization for data your own service wrote and still controls.

## Measure it
Prove the defenses with negative tests: a fetch to an internal IP must be refused; requests for `../../etc/passwd`, `%2e%2e/config` and absolute paths must all return not-found without touching the filesystem outside base; a mutated serialized blob must fail schema validation, never load. Run these tests in CI so refactors cannot silently remove the checks.

## Best practices
- Allowlist outbound URL scheme and host; deny everything else by default.
- Canonicalize (decode + normalize) before any prefix or extension check on paths.
- Prefer server-generated filenames; treat user-supplied names as untrusted hints at most.
- Use JSON + schema validation for untrusted structured data.
- Log every allowlist/canonicalization rejection with the raw input for investigation.

## Common mistakes
- Checking for the literal substring `..` instead of canonicalizing — encoded or nested escapes slip past.
- Allowlisting hosts but forgetting redirects, which bounce the fetch to an internal address.
- Deserializing session or cache blobs from user-writable storage with a reconstructing loader.
- Building paths with string concatenation and validating only the file extension.
- Treating `JSON.parse` of a huge payload as safe while ignoring resource exhaustion (size limits are validation too).

## Production considerations
- Run outbound fetchers with network policies that make internal ranges unreachable anyway — defense in depth behind the allowlist.
- Configure file servers to resolve symlinks and jail them to the serving root.
- Version your persisted data formats so schema migrations are explicit, not accidental deserialization drift.
- Alert on traversal-pattern rejections in aggregate: sustained probing usually precedes a targeted attempt.

examples.name: safe-path-join.js

exercise.prompt: Build the path traversal defender (mirrors this app's own validator): decode the requested path, split into segments, drop empty, dot and dot-dot segments, and render allow or deny — deny when any parent-dir segment was detected in the raw request (suspicious probing) or when the resolved path would leave uploads/. Show the sanitized path for allowed requests. Implement isSuspicious and sanitize.
hints: Parent-dir tricks: .. or %2e%2e appearing in the raw string — check both.
sanitize must decodeURIComponent first, then filter segments equal to empty string, . or ...
A leading / would make the join start outside BASE; make sure absolute input is also neutralized.

questions.prompt: Why must a path be canonicalized before the prefix check against an allowed directory?
options: To make the path shorter for logging
Because encoded and dotted segments are aliases that only resolve to their real meaning during canonicalization
Because the filesystem rejects non-canonical paths
To fix the file's read permissions
questions.explanation: Raw-string checks can be fooled by %2e%2e, doubled slashes or dot segments; after canonicalization every alias has become its real path, so the prefix check is meaningful.

questions.prompt: What makes SSRF possible even when the target server is not public?
options: The attacker's browser forwards packets into the internal network
The vulnerable server itself fetches the attacker-chosen URL from inside the network
questions.explanation: SSRF abuses the server's own network position: the attacker supplies the URL, and your server — which can reach internal services — makes the request for them.
